div.p: Stella Kramer’s 1979 Vol. 2 edition of STELAZINE is a nonlinear compilation of Seattle punk scene goings-on, conveyed through a variety of interviews (conducted by Kramer herself), prose snippets, absurd poetry, and collage-esque photography and graphic layouts. Kramer is a local punk-scene legend and Pulitzer Prize-winning photo-journalist, who first had thoughts of developing a published zine after moving to Seattle in 1976 and becoming a part of the then-small punk-scene through informally writing reviews of local shows. It is through STELAZINE that Kramer blossomed the niche-punk and alternative scene of Seattle into the iconic focal point of music it is today.

This digital edition of Kramer’s STELAZINE hopes to make the zine more accessible to those who want to experience Kramer’s work. Previously, this was only accessible in print. We hope that by digitizing this physical media, it breathes new life into the work and words that were published almost 50 years ago. The content, interviews, and art contained in the zine open a door to the Seattle punk scene as it was in the 70s. These never-before-seen interviews with Poly Styrene (of X-Ray Spex) and Paul Simonon (The Clash) offer unique and interesting takes on not only their music, but the Seattle music scene—all of which would be lost to time without this zine. While it is difficult to digitally represent a zine that was not created with digitization in mind, we hope that the work we do here will incentivize people to perhaps go down to the Special Collections themselves to take a look at this zine and the many other amazing works that they house.

This zine includes quite a few spelling errors, which we elected to correct as an editorial team. We decided that the errors were not necessary to include in our digitized zine, and the integrity of the text is still retained with the corrections. We also elected to censor racial slurs by keeping the first letter and replacing the rest with asterisks. It may have been acceptable to type out the full word when this zine was published in the 70s, but the 2026 editing team did not feel comfortable keeping those uncensored slurs in our edition. The text still comes across in the same way with this censorship, and no readability is lost.

div.p: It took three days of massive telephoning. First to Epic Records in New York. Then to LA. Then to Vancouver. But I was determined to see them and talk to them.

I finally connected with road manager Johnny Green in Vancouver, and after countless phone calls to their hotel, I found Caroline Coon. It wasn’t until the day of the show that things were arranged, but it was worth it. A lesson for all: Go directly to the band.
I was allowed backstage after the show and waited around talking. Finally I was ushered into a small dressing room to talk to Paul.
I entered, after stepping over Joe, Mick, and Topper who were being interviewed by some asshole from the straight press.
Paul was sitting on a leopard-covered couch in the corner ,all in black. Wearing sunglasses. He intimidated me at first, as I sat on the floor next to him.

But as the interview went on I relaxed and so did he. Too bad we were cut off just as we started to relax. So read on. This is a report about the Clash’s first gig in North America. All the way from January to you.
S: What did you think of the show?
PAUL: It’s alright. It’s okay. We weren’t too bad for a first one, ‘cause usually we’re a bit rusty. We never played Canada or America before, so it’s pretty new.
S: How do you prepare for a show, because you play really hard. You seem to expend all of your energy…
PAUL: I dunno. Sometimes, it depends… what we’ve been doing the last couple of days is swimming. We had a game of football with the local kids ‘round here.
S: I hear you’re good.
PAUL: Yeah, we’re alright. We don’t overdo it–like drugs. I don’t have enough time for that. Makes me sleepy, anyway. So we don’t go in for all that.
S: What are you thinking about when you are on stage? The song you’re playing?
PAUL: What the next chord is! (Laughter)
S: Do you notice the crowd alot?
PAUL: Yeah, quite alot. It’s pretty hard not to.
S: Some people get so involved with the music, that they don’t see the crowd... lights in their eyes and all...
PAUL: I dunno. I look at both. I gotta look down at what I’m playing anyhow, ‘cause I might hit the wrong note. It’s good fun though.
S: You looked like you were having a really good time.
PAUL: It’s alright.
S: Do you improvise?
PAUL: Yeah, sometimes. Sometimes I have to ‘cause I can’t remember the rest… But seriously. Sometimes I do, you know just to change it around a bit.
S: Caroline said you don’t get much airplay in England
PAUL: Not much. We had a terrible time trying to get airplay and all that. But everybody would buy our records, but there’d be no airplay. But since our last album came out it’s increased sligh-tly.
S: Do you tour alot in England?
PAUL: Quote alot, yeah.
S: So that’s how people hear your music?
PAUL: Yeah. We’re sort of like tops in England.
S: You must get interviewed alot.
PAUL: Yeah, quite alot.
S: Do you like it?
PAUL: I don’t mind. I quite enjoy it sometimes. I think it’s alright. It sort of makes you re-examine your beliefs on things. All sorts of things, you know.
S: Caroline said you wanted opening bands to be female...
PAUL:Yeah
S: Is that with all the US gigs?

PAUL: I don’t know. Not all of them, don’t think. But as many as possible. It’s good for a change. Usually people see just blokes getting up on stage all the time. If there’s girls getting up it makes a change, and it’s like… it’s pretty good ‘cause it encourages other girls to be in groups, and there ain’t really enough girls in groups these days it seems.
S: It’s true. Are you going to get a chance to see the country?
PAUL: We spent the last three days here, walked around and like checked the place out.
S: Never been here before?

PAUL: No, never. And generally all the other shows we’ve got ‘round the country we’ll have a couple of days off. Not actually off, ‘cause we’ll have interviews to do. There’ll be an hour off here or there, so we’ll get out as much as possible and have a look around.
S: Is it hard keeping contact with your audience?

PAUL: It’s not hard at all. Just get out of your room and walk down the street, you know. That’s what I do. That’s what we all do, even when we’re back in London. People come up to us and talk to us. I quite enjoy that. It’s like having lots of friends.
S: People aren’t afraid to approach you?
PAUL: I don’t know. Sometimes and sometimes not. It’s all down to the actual person and how much they want to meet you, I suppose.
S: Did you organize the tour? Or how much was it organized by the record company?

PAUL: They sort of like… we decided where to play. Actually Caroline and an agency decided where to play. We can say we don’t want to play there, or whatever, but we never say that anyway… It’s the record company that at the mo-ment puts up the money for us to tour; so have Bo Diddley on the tour.
S: They determine how much the tickets cost?

PAUL: To a certain extent..not too much. At the moment, because it’s the first tour that we’ve done, I suppose. They-’re generally smaller places we’re playing, and not too many people know about us, so the money we have to charge on the door (‘cause we have to pay for the road crew, lights, the PA…)- on the next tour it will probably be more self-supporting, where with this tour CBS is paying quite alot.
S: Do you find it different than you expected working with a record company? You’ve done two albums now, ad as far as bands fo, you’re in a more comfortable position...

PAUL: Well, not really. We have alot of fights with the record company. There’s nothing you can do about it really, you just keep fighting. If you sign to a small record company… If we signed to a small record company we probably wouldn’t be here now, and probably half of the people in Britain and here and wherever wouldn’t have heard our records… It’s a choice. We never wanted to be a small or cult band. We wanted to be on top, you know?

S: You’re new record has things which stick out more than on the first album. PAUL: Yeah, I dunno. I think it’s cot it in the first album as well, except you can’t hear it too well, ‘cause of the way ti was recorded. Whereas now it sounds alot clearer. There’s more depth in the record, so you can hear more in it.
S: Are you still learning how to record? I assume with the second album you went into a good studio...

PAUL: Well, no. We went into a studio that was as good as the first one we went into, except there are certain things you can do with microphones, and the type of cabinet–amplifier you use. When we recorded the first album we just had microphones up against each amplifier, and played it, and that was it. Whereas on the second album we had microphones up against the amps as well as two microphones at the end of the big room… so it’s got ambiance.
S: Do you like recording?
PAUL: It’s alright. It’s not bad. It’s a bit boring sometimes.
S: Do you like touring?
PAUL: Yeah, it’s pretty good fun, ‘cause you go to alot of different places.
S: Do you get tired of playing the same songs over and over again?
PAUL: No. They always sem to be a bit different.
S: Do you rehearse alot?
PAUL: Generally quite alot. It depends if we need to.

S: Even though you have alot of fans, and your album is doing well, do you still have problems with rehearsal studios? I mean alot of bands can’t find studios, and if they do people don’t want them to play loud...

PAUL: We did when we first started. But when we signed… joined up with Bernie Rhodes, our old manager, he got a rehearsal studio together for us. It was our own one so we could rehearse and be as loud as possible. Whereas lately we got rid of him and we’ve had problems getting a hold of rehearsal halls.
S: Do you consider the band the same as it’s been all along?
PAUL: Yeah. It’s just we can play better now.
S: That must be a good feeling.
PAUL: Yeah, it’s pretty good.

p.hi: [Pause while Topper gets a light for a cigarette]

div.p: S: What kind of directions are you looking to take with the band? I understand you want to come back and tour in June.
PAUL: Yeah, do a larger one. This is a small one really; just to see how it goes, I suppose.
S: Do you want to go to, say, Japan?
PAUL: Yeah. We’d like to go everywhere… As much as possible. We never really wanted to be stuck in London all the time. We all wanted to play everywhere.
S: How much chance do you think there is for your music to get on the radio? In London the charts are so much different than they are here. Here it’s real disappointing.
PAUL: Someday it’s bound to. Probably when we give up they’ll start playing it When we decide to do something else.
S: What kind of music do you listen to?
PAUL: Umm… sort of anything really. But generally I listen to old stuff like rockabilly and like Bo Diddley and Little Richard, and stuff like that. I like that a lot. And reggae, you know.
S: Did you find it hard to listen to the bass?
PAUL: First I did. First six months it was really difficult. Then after awhile I played along with records and it got easier and easier.
S: You just learned off of records? You didn’t take lessons?
PAUL: No, not proper lessons.
S: What made you decide to play bass?
PAUL: Umm..... ‘Cause it’s easier to learn. It’s the quickest one you can learn. You can just strum a note and after awhile when you get better you can start to do little tunes.
S: What kind of bass do you play?
PAUL: Fender. It’s generally the most reliable.
S: Are there alot of bands in England still forming; alot of bands still popping up, or has it leveled out?
PAUL: It’s sort of leveled out a but, but there are still new bands coming up here and there.
S: Younger bands?
PAUL: Who?
S: Younger bands?
PAUL: I thought you said yoga bands.....
S: Younger. Like 15, 16….
PAUL: It sort of varies, you know. There’s that sort of younger….really younger groups, and then sort of older groups. It’s sort of even out, but there are still groups forming.

S: Do you think it was easier for you..I don’t know how much you know about what goes on in the US, but most bands, especially bands on the east coast have trouble getting signed. It seemed that British bands had an easier time getting signed after awhile.

figure.figDesc: Another picture of Paul taken during the interview.

div.p: PAUL: Yeah, I think the strange thing was, ‘cause like when we first started, no record company or anybody like that would come near us. But we weren’t going to go to them. They’d have to come to us. The same with journalists and things like that; the big music papers in England.
S: Do you find it hard to keep the band going?
PAUL: Keep the band going?
S: Is it easy to maintain?
PAUL: It’s quite easy. We sort of get on alright. Don’t have any problems.
S: You’re all friends?
PAUL: Yeah, pretty good friends.
S: Hang around together when you’re not playing?
PAUL: Sometimes we do. Not too much, ‘cause we’d get really bored of each other and start fighting.
S: How much time to you spend on the band?
PAUL: Generally all of me time. Most of me time.
S: Do you write any music?
PAUL: Not as yet, but I’m starting to. I-’ve been reading loads of books lately to get my English better.
S: Like what?
PAUL: George Orwell, Aldous Huxley...
S: Do you go to movies?
PAUL: Yeah, I go to pictures quite alot. Quite a few good films I’ve seen lately. I’ve seen crappy ones too, like superman. It’s the worst one I’ve ever seen.. (Laughs)
S: Someone just told me it’s great.

PAUL: It’s stupid. It’s funny. I mean it’s good in the end. There are real choppy bits and real funny bits. There’s a bit where he’s running along trying to beat the train and they lift him up about an inch off the ground and his legs are going like this (demonstrates racing legs), and they do it in fast motion. It’s really hilarious.
S: Did they take stuff away from you at the border?
PAUL: They never saw mine (bondage gear) They took their (the rest of the band’s) stuff, but they never saw mine.
S: You hid yours?
PAUL: Yeah. I was walking around the airport like this (pulls his jacket over his face and skulks along)...(Laughter)
S: They didn’t come up to you?
PAUL: Well, they searched through my stuff but they didn’t find it. I was too clever (Laughter).
S: So their stuff was confiscated?
PAUL: Yeah. We got it back though.
S: What did they think you were going to do with it? Did they really think they were deadly weapons?
PAUL: I dunno.... The police....
S: Do you get hassled by the police alot
PAUL: Generally in England we do.
S: Do you get arrested alot?
PAUL: Sometimes.

p.hi: (At this point road manager Johnny Green broke up the interviews. We all grab the last bits of food in the dressing room and leave).

div.head: in VANCOUVER
div.p: This had to be the biggest thing to happen in too long a time. The Clash were playing near home, Vancouver to be exact. The first stop of their N. American tour. We came by the carloads.
The Commodore is a good place for a show. It's an old ballroom, with enough floor space for everyone to get involved. Even enough room for those who chose to be on the outside of this event.

The atmosphere was charged, waiting to explode. The Dishrags opened with a well-recieved set. They have the distinction of being one of the only three-piece and all-girl bands in these parts. They delivered a strong, unpretentious, confident performance. What a refreshing sight!
The Dishrags are not a "melodic" band. But they are powerful and a whole lot better than many others. A good choice for setting the pace of the night.

After their impressive set they were off. I wished they had played more. Especially instead of Bo Diddley. Perhaps I'm being disrespectful, but he bored me. The same old jams, held out until your mind numbs to the sound. This was the time for the other half of the crowd to have their fun. For most it was a time to circulate and await the arrival of the Clash.

It seemed like forever until the stage was cleared and ready to go. Barriers were set up before the stage, and a mad pushing scene began. People were caught between the stage and the barricades; tension was mounting. Bouncers were abusive and manhandled a number of people just trying to get some air. I had jumped on stage to avoid the crush only to be knocked down by a snarling stage hand. But enough. The bomb was ticking....
Then came the band. The dance floor became a mass of bodies and arms, also trying to get close, to get the ultimate rush off the band.

They ran on stage; Topper in yellow, Mick and Paul in black and white, Joe in red. They looked almost well-dressed–no letters. Primary colors; blocks of color focusing eyes on the unit. The floor began to bounce under the pressure, as the band ripped into their first song. All the time I had been hoping to hear one particular song, and as if to win me permanently over to their side (how did they know?), they opened with "Complete Control". It was almost too much.

My first impressions were of Topper: commanding such attention with his power drumming. He looked so skinny I expected his drumming to reflect that. A wonderful contradiction. He never let up, pushing the beat relentlessly, Martial arts translated into an art you could hear. Like carpet bombing, the earth shakes from the impact.
Mick taking stances on his side of the stage. Then running from one end to the other. He wouldn't stand still. The whole band forced your attention even beyond the music with their actions....
Assaultive. Confrontive. Sweeping up the audience with their music and movements until you were almost on stage with them. There is no way to deny the comparisons with an army.

Mick's guitar is like a weapon; spraying the audience with bullets. Like the frontal attacker. There is also an unmistakeable quality of joy in his playing. Of course he's serious, but you can't help being affected by his happiness in playing. It is infectious. He smiles, dances with the beat, runs in place keeping the beat.

Paul is a ferocious bass player. he drives it, pushing it into your face. No relief. He stands on the edge of the stage--you get the feeling he wants to jump off. Not content with the boundaries set before him. He has a way of dancing with the music. Pumping his body and his bass in perfect time. Sensuous.

He seems as if he's painting. Playing the bass as if it's a brush against canvas of air. It's so electric, you can feel the pull. As if the bass would fly out into the crowd. I get the feeling his playing has considerably improved. He is one hell of a bassist.

While Paul's acrobatics might not be as pronounced as Mick's, he doesn't lay back. He is the supporting division. He fills in the holes of the attack. Tall and lean (skinny); a riveting intenseness. Mesmerizing. Playing off Mick. The floor is bending under the excitement.

Watching the Clash is like being subjected to a never-ending barrage of newsreels. The shouting, the indignation, the horror, the anger; Joe raves about it all. Contempt spitting from his body like an outraged person viewing the world before him. Sometimes his visions are sly, sometimes obscure-- always immediate. He leans forward, curling his body around the mike stand like a cobra poised to strike. Sometimes the bite is still unexpected.

His guitar is there--the constant buzz of electrical wires. Always there... sometimes even the guitar is his enemy as he pushes it aside--trying to get closer to what he sees. His voice battering your conscience.

The Clash are a phenomenon. And, they played everything. From "Safe European Home", and the rest of the new album to "White Man", "I Fought The Law", "Clash City Rockers", and songs from the first album: “Janie Jones", "Garageland", "Career Opportunities", "White Riot", "I’m So Bored With The USA". Sixteen songs and two encores.

We were even treated to Mick singing "Stay Free". Even a new song: "Garbage" “Written by our good friend Barry Manilow", said Joe..."I been studying the charts/I've been using my mind and imagination…”

By the end the sound had begun to disintegrate. The band had gone beyond what anyone expected. They had given us everything possible. All the excitement, all the music, all the power we had a right to expect. Make no mistake about it: The Clash delivered.
When it was over no one moved. We all knew it had to end. But I didn't feel a lack. I felt as though I had eaten a 12 course dinner. The tastes, the sights, the sensuousness remained.
The Clash are a vision.

div.head: POLY STYRENE X-RAY-SPEX CHATS w/Neva Chonin
div.p: Over the past year, X-Ray Spex have grown from a band with a larger than average cult following into one of the brightest hopes on the current rock scene. Their rise to the top, which began in 1977 with their appearance on the legendary “Live at the Roxy” album, and is still peaking with the release of their own LP, “Germ Free Adolescents”, comes as no surprise to those who have actually seen Spex in action and felt the sheer power of the group.

Me, I can still remember the first time I saw the live… It was at the Marquee one cold night in the fall of ‘77. I was feeling extremely under the weather due to a slight case of frostbite and malnutrition, and was dead certain that nothing shore of a minor earthquake would be successful in dragging me out of my self-induced stupor.

What I failed to realize was that seeing Poly Styrene on stage is synonymous with being caught in a minor earthquake (or a major one at that). Both experiences shake you up considerably. With her hair in braids and teeth in braces, not only did she get me up and dancing (no small feat in the steam-bath, sardine tin atmosphere of the Marquee) but gave my spirits a much needed boost as well. Nor was I alone in my enthusiasm, as the audience proved by madly pogoing in the limited space available. The evening climaxes with Sid Vicious momentarily abandoning Nancy to leap onstage for the final chorus of “Oh Bonadge, Up Yours”! Within seconds the rest of the kids followed suit and the club exploded into uncontrollable chaos. And you wonder why I love this band?

A few months after that memorable show, I sat down with Poly in the kitchen of her home in south London and listened as she traced back through the history of the British scene, from the early days at the Roxy Club, where she and Johnny Rotten were labeled “n****** lovers” for dancing to reggae music (wasn’t fashionable yet, y’see), through the so-called Summer of Hate when press inspired violence erupted between the punks and the Teddy Boys. Both Poly and I have had late nights with little sleep and so experience a bit of difficulty in coping with the interview situation; hence half the time is spent in giggles and nonsensical remarks. The comprehensible parts read thusly...
NEVA: What types of places did you play at the very beginning?
div.outputRendition: POLY: Our first gig was at the Roxy in Covent Garden. That place was one of the reasons that we were able to get our act together, because it was the only place in London where you could be seen…When it opened up the basic principle was to give any band the opportunity to play and have people come down to see them. That’s why it was a great club. But different people took it over–the guy who originally made it what it was got kicked out and the owners started running it. It lost all the atmosphere and just got ‘orrible.
div.p: NEVA: Hasn’t that happened to the whole movement, though? Now there’s grown-ups singing with record companies and suddenly going punk overnight.
POLY: I suppose it has changed a bit, but then everything changes, doesn't it? I don’t like these bands that record companies put together, but you can suss ‘em out a mile away, anyway.
NEVA: Are you interested in appealing to a wide variety of people?

POLY: If you’ve got something to say you should want to say it to as many people as possible, you shouldn’t worry about who it is, you know. To me it’s music…I mean, “Punk” rock…..I guess it’s good ‘cause you need a word to identify yourself. But even within that I’m still me.
NEVA: Alot of originality has disappeared, it seems. Everyone dresses alike.

POLY: Yeah, we’re trying to break away from all that. I never do what anybody else does, I always do what I want. But it’s inevitable that they’re going to do it up to appoint ‘cause they want to identify with something, you see. They’re desperately trying to identify themselves with something so they can think “Ah, that’s it–I’ve found my niche. If i put on this shirt or that, I’ll be accepted by punks. I’ll be a punk.” All they have to realize is that they can only be accepted by themselves. Self-confidence is the most important thing. To come out of yourself and just do what you like and don’t worry about being accepted by anyone. So up to a point you can slag them off, but up to another point you cannot, ‘cause you have to look at it from both sides of the coin. You can’t judge anybody from yourself—-you can’t just say, “Oh, they should be doing this and that and they should be doing what I’m doing.” ‘Cause if they was then they’d be copying you, you see. They don’t have to do that.. If they want to be posers, then that’s alright as long as they know they’re posing and say “Yeah, I’m a poser, so what? Big deal!” As long as they know they are. It’s only when they don’t know that they get into a state of confusion! People have to get into it at different levels. If they want to get totally involved that’s fine, and if they just want to get into it just for fun then that’s alright too. There’s more to it as well, apart from that, but they should just take what they want from it from their own personal point of view.
NEVA: What was it like during the Punk Ted war in the summer of ‘77?

POLY: I used to work in a stall in the Beaufort Market, selling punk clothes and that, and the Teds used to come down every Saturday and smash the windows. It got really violent down there, due to the papers. There was no hating each other till the papers wrote about it. As soon as they wrote about violence on Kings Road, there was violence on the Kings Road… And there was all these tourists from all over the world, Americans, Swedes, standing on the other side watching it and taking pictures. They would all come to the Kings Road every Saturday to watch Punks vs Teds. That was a big thing that summer.
NEVA: What were the fights like?
POLY: They weren’t really all that bad. Every Saturday at 2:00 a big gang of Teds would come up from Sloane Square and meet with a big gang of punks and sometimes somebody would get knifed.
NEVA: Does it bother you being labeled as a “girl singer” rather than simply a singer, period?

POLY: Well the thing is, I don’t think of myself as a boy or girl, I think of myself as a person, just an individual in my own right. I don’t compare myself with other girls, so it don’t make no difference to me if the press want to compare me with other girls, ‘cause I know it’s rubbish and it can’t affect me.
NEVA: What do you do if someone in the audience is giving you a hard time?

POLY: I dunno, it depends on the situation. One bloke, a rugby player type came onstage once and tried to pick me up and I just hit him over the head with the mikestand. He got off quick! He didn’t know what hit him ‘cause he thought I was going to scream or cry or something, but I just turned ‘round and went after him and chased him off stage!
NEVA: Do you enjoy playing the states?

POLY: Yeah, I’m interested in playing anywhere. A lot of people say, “Oh, Yanks–they got no culture.” But that’s bullshit. You got a culture of your own and just ‘cause it’s a new one… That’s like the Africans saying the Jamaicans ain’t got culture.
NEVA: Ours is a very plastic culture.
POLY: That don’t worry me. I think this plastic culture is quite a laugh, and I’m quite into it ‘cause it’s real, it’s happening now.
NEVA: Which are your favorites from the New York bands?

POLY: So far I haven’t really liked any of them, but maybe that’s because alot of them are older, and I only really like the young groups—’cause to me that’s what it should be about. So if there was young New York groups I’d probably like them, but they’re all quite old and they come from another period. I can’t really relate to it.
NEVA: What kind of music do you like then?

div.p: There are three established clubs in the city:CBGB's, Max's, and Hurrah All week music. Admission is $4 to $6 depending on the day. Count on seeing anyone. It's the crowd that can sway your feelings. CB's is overrun with tourists eager for a glimpse of "new wave". You can't get out of your seat so where's the fun? Max's is better, although the sound isn't as good. Th- ere's a coldness about it to me. Hur- rah's is highly considered by people in the city. Getting better. Then there are the week-end clubs... Mudd Club, Club 57, Club Hollywood... Studio 10 and sometimes Trax. Studio 10 is a Yippie club in the west Vill- age. Club 57 is gaining prominence--- strong shows, good atmosphere and go- od fun. Admission is $4. One of the places to go to. Mudd Club is the most highly prais- ed. With acoustics rumored as being designed by the one and only Eno--- it is new and rising fast. Set in the Soho area it provides weekend entert- ainment of the most novel kind. Cons- tant choices.

Clubs advertize in the newspapers: Village Voice and Shoh Weekly. Other- wise you see wall posters. few bands print posters. New bands never do. We in Seattle have relied on wall posters like a great wall of informa¬ tion. But we have not had media acce- ptance. The price you pay for being a provincial city... Poster artwork runs the gamut from imaginative to boring. Too few of the former, too much of the latter. Opinions are worn on lapels in this city. Store bought, profuse. Why make them when you can buy them? The star- kest difference here is the accepti- bility of new wave. You can hang out in the East Villa- ge: Manic Panic (and talk to Snooky).. Trash & Vaudeville, Defiant pose... Or to the West Village and the Bowery¬ Next Empire and Revenge, Bookstores.. Record stores—the best being Village Oldies, where you can hear reggae on the radio, and any band you care to on the stereo. Even clothing if you're just in from the 'burbs.... Visit Punk Mag or the Rocker. Find

book stores full of fanzines. It's all here. A decent selection of local fanzin- es (besides the big two). Esther too eclectic, or too "in scene". The best are "Beat It" and "No"-the latter be ing crammed with the impact of eight million images, impact, writing and ? Find it. Lesser interesting ones inc- lude: the in-joke "Skull Damage" for affecionados exclusively; "Smegma'-- xerox and fun, and "2+2= 3 or 4 or 5 or 6 or 7 or 8 or 9" -done by Susan Springfield of the Erasers. As bori- ing as her band and as trite. Everyone wears black leather. Youre either punk or pop. Take it as you like. Lots of clothes for the clothes conscious. Lots of celebrities. Like most towns the people are spl- it. A and B lists of bands depend on who you're talking to. Too many imit- ations: of Patti, of the Heads, of our boys from OHIO. Some are fun. The au- diences are made up of old-timers, those who are or have been in bands. A few wide-eyed kids figuring they've stumbled onto something BIG. Then th-

ere are the tourists. Lots of bands are working on relea sing vinyl It helps the CB's puts out albums (the next one should be on the racks soon, and is worth picking up-ED.) People from established ban- ds will produce newer bands. It's im- pressive. There is a third generation gaining strength in the club scene. div.p: I wanted to interview Laura after hearing Student Teachers at CBGB's, and being impressed with her drumming. Laura is a stand-out destined to make a name for herself. The interview was conducted at an apartment in Manhattan which Laura shares with Jimmy "The Housepainter Destri". We talked in the living room/bedroom, amid a ringing telephone and Laura's sister. The one window on the room had a teriffic view of the city.......
S:How long have you been playing drums?
L:A year.
S:That's all?

L:Year, only a year. I took lessons for about four or five months and then I stopped. We started playing alot more, having alot of gigs. It takes money, so I never got around to picking up lessons again. So I took them for a few months, then just played along by myself, and watched other drummers, and picked up tips from friends of mine. I still have alot to learn.
S:How old are you?
L:17. We're a very young band.
S:I could tell.
L:I just turned 17 in December.
S:Were you instrumental in forming the band?

L:Yeah, well sort of. It all started with my keyboard player, Bill, my bass player and myself who had a band at one time. But it was just an idea. I didn't play drums at the time, and she hadn't played bass, but we liked the idea of getting a band together.. We talked about it for about a year.. Then my keyboard player became very good friends with the singer, David. David said he had this guitarist friend, and brought him along. We had a photo session evenbefore we rehearsed, 'cause we all liked the way the other looked.
S:What's the name of your guitarist?

L:Phillip Shelley. We had this photo session... We knew nothing! We were just forming this band. Nobody knew what they wanted to do. We finally got our first rehearsal together. Slowly things started getting along, and we played our first gig at my high school.
S:Which one?

L:It's Friend's Seminary on E. 16th.. It's a private H.S. A joke, but we played a concert just to get the feel of playing in front of people. Our friends The Blessed came to see us ...They liked us, and were playing the next Sunday as Max's and said: "Why don't you open for us?" So we went to Max's (we knew the booking agent), and said:"Why don'cha let us do this?" She said fine. We didn't get billed or anything. It was like an audition for the club. They really liked us so we got another gig there a couple of weeks later. It started like that. It was slow at first at the beginning, but then we found ouselves playing three or four gigs a month. Things started going very fast. Then we had a gig at Max's. Bill came up and said, Jimmy Destri wants to take us into the studio. What do you think?" I said sure. We were all really excited. He came to lots of rehearsals and went over the songs, & we recorded in the middle of last July. Recorded our single, which isn't out yet,but should be soon.
S:What songs?
L:"Christmas Weather" and "The Quake"
S:"The Quake" seems to be a popular song.
L:Yeah, that's the one Bill and I write. The major songwriters are Bill & Phillip, which is strange, 'cause they write in completely differnt ways
S:Was that your drumkit you used at CB's?
L:No.It was Jane's of the Erasers. It is an incredible drum kit. A vintage Pearl.
S:It was miked well.
JD:Thank you.
S:Yeah, my friend really liked the sound of the tom-toms.
JD:Thanks.
L:It's a beautiful set. Her boyfriend bought it for her.
S:We should all be so lucky.
L:Yeah, we shoud have.....
JD:Boyfriends who buy drum sets!
S:DO you have your own kit?

L:Sort of. I'm losing it rapidly. I bought a couple of drums from the Mumps drummer. Used drums 'cause I had no money. I bought a snare and two toms and a bass drum--all for $200... Then we got into a fight and he took them back. I's all ridiculous. But usually I just borrow. A lot of people are very generous in lending me their stuff. If you're careful and responsible.
S:What made you decide to learn drums.

L:The great question...Once I said to a friend I have Three reasons. One, I like to sweat. Two, Blondies drummer Clen who is an amazing drummer. I really look up to him. I'd just like to play like that. I had another reason- it's an obscure reason, but whenever I was listening to a song I would speciffically listen to the beat. Of course its the beat that captures you. But it came consious to me... Not just listening to the beat and dancing, but I was ignoring the guitars and keyboards and voices and stuff. It became extremely consious to me, and I went zing! I just feel there should be more female drummers. If you feel you can handle it.
S:I noticed with your playing that you really keep the beat of the song going. I had the feeling that if you weren't playing the rest of it would fall apart.
L:(Laughter)Yeah, I get that reaction alot.
S:You're also really strong in directing the music, which is something not many drummers do.

L:Oh thank you. (Self-consious, nervous laughter). I don't even know if I'm consious of that. I don't know. I get real nervous, 'cause I know that whenever we do badly in a song I know that I've done badly. I just automatically assume it's me all the way. If the whole song falls apart I know its been me. I can just feel it. But I don't go out there and say... "I'm gonna direct this song!" I guess it just happens.
S:It's spontaneous...What's going on with the record?
L:Well, good question. As far as the record's concered, it's been sold. To Red Star Records who have expressed extreme intrest in us, but haven't moved their asses. So they bought our single.
S:New blood.
L:Yes. Alot of interest has come, but we get impatient. We intend to work hard enough to get something. We feel we can. It gets very tough, you know. But I have alot of optimistic hopes.
S:So you have a job outside of the band?
L:Not at the moment 'cause I've got school. I'm in my last year of H.S-- Hi! mom. And so it gets very difficult. I'm looking for one. I need the money.
S:How do you feel when you're playing. Do you think of anything specific?

L:Yes. First of all I think about whats going on. Like I'm listening to the stuff and how and how the songs are going . And then I try and put myself in an objective place. Like, if I was out in the audience and I was listening to this song, what would I think? Would I like it? 'Cause a couple of our songs are like weird! Then of course, I think about the important people who might be out there and what their reactions are.
S:You want commercial success with your music?

L:I guess it would be nice. I'm confused about that stuff, because I'm not quite sure what I want. I'm not quite sure if I want money, or if I just want fame or I just want to play rock and roll all the time--play drums. Or, just be a famous drummer.
S:Are you success oriented?

L:I always wanted to play in a band.. ALways. Always wanted to play drums. I never even considered doing anything else, like singing. (Her sister cuts in:"Except when ya wanted to be a bassoon player...")
L:You know, school music.
S: Is it difficult being so young?

L:Yes. Yes and no. Sometimes it's fun lens are we're young and I guess a litte naive. We feel separated from the musicians who are 24, 25---who've been playing a long time. The Erasers are all 27, 28--old age land (Laughter) We still get the look ike we're little kids having fun, who are pretty accomplished for our age. But there'r still seperations. (To Jimmy) Well.. you're old!!
JD:Yeah, but I've made it already.
L:I just come up with a good title for a song and write from that. "The Quake" was written from a personal experience becuase I go to a Quaker school and I was kicked out.
S:Why?

L:Because I was living alone last year without my parents and they didn't like it. I was living with my bass player, and The Blessed, and half of New York rock was in my apartment. So it was a crazy lifestyle.
S:Talk about your drumming..your style...things like that. What kind of a kit do you want?

L:It's very hard. Maybe a Premier. Maybe a good Pearl set. I dream about having a great drum set Premier would probably be what I'd get. They're very sturdy. One of my problems with player is that my right arm--I play alot of tight beats and it hurts when I'm playing. I don't get a chance to exercise it enough playing drums because I only have access to a studio once in awhile. When I play, one of my problems is to not get physically or phychologicallly upset about the pain goig through my arm. If I get upset. I start losing the beat. I start getting crazy. So one of my problems is to learn to keep calm and paced.
S:Do you do any kind of exercises?

L:Yeah. Just before I play I take the two metal practice sticks and I shake them, keeping the arm straight, as fast as I can. My tendon gets really sore, but loose. It's also a matter of playing correctly. I can slip into not playing correctly and it can hurt and I start using my arm. One ting I do is keep tha wrist really loose and keep playing with the wrist. That's the only physical problem I have with playing. I have aninsecurity about drumming. People say, "You're really good, one of the best female drummers I've seen. But I'm not happy with myself yet. I get very insecure about my stle. I have a very simple and straightforward style at the moment, because I am not sure how to do other things. I don't wanna get crazy and do ten million rolls like those rock and roll drummers do. That's a waste. It's just boring.
S:Whose drumming do you like?
L:Well, Clem Burke is my idol. I also like Chris Frantz (T. Heads-Ed.). Right now I'm following his style which is very straightforward. There are no female drummers that I know that I like.
S:What are some of your influences?
L:Jimmy. Thank god he's in the shower. He influences me a lot. I'm always around Blondies and their success. I wa-

div.p: MIKI ZONE ZOO/the dots COME ON
Tonight it’s Max's. A chance to see local luminaries. They come to see the headliner….

But first The Dots. A four-piece young band. Alison East is one of the best new guitarists I have seen.. She can rock! What a personality! Eyes and mouth wide open; she dances and jerks her hands Spikey hair... like the caucasians in Japanese comics. She is frozen in mid-second as if always surprised.
A great racing guitar sound. Sharp and clean. Good bass

The band's a bit too rock and roll I wish they were more original. Their songs are delivered well, with crispness. Lots of hooks. "Let Me Take You Out To Lunch” stands out. But, they have too many love songs. Nothing new–the male influence?
The singer is not dangerous looking more like deranged. A mad scientist?? He looks and moves furtively. Too much heavy metal music involved…But Alison is so fresh!
Now for the crowd pleasers…..Miki Zone Zoo (formerly the Fast). They look like an LA Band. Well dressed.. good moves…Flash….
A crisp sound with a look to match. Black and white. Stripes and solids. Taking up the stage like a set sculpture. Even the negative spaces are filled.
MZZ is a band which operates on hyper kinetic energy. Everything is fast. Why wait when we’ll all be gone in a minute? A unit, yet strong individuals pierce through.

The wildest of all is the infamous Miki Zone, guitarist extraordinaire.. With the drummer bashing away at rhythm, the bass player peering out from under long dark bangs, and the singer hopping around like he’s barefoot on
coals, Miki creates the ultimate movement and grips his side of the stage with a wall of force.

A wild player and a visual delight. Miki grimaces, pouts, pounds his head, jumps, hops, spins and camps–all the while playing inspirational guitar. A riveting performer. So slim and dark with clothes almost too big for him: a baggy pin-striped suit with a spider on the lapel.
The singer is wild; Ricky Ricardo with a dash of Valentino. This band’s so obviously having fun!

The hottest number is “The Kids Just Wanna Dance”, better than any shit disco number to get you on your feet. I mean it isn’t just a great song, it’s a tour-de-force for Miki. He takes off his guitar in the middle, hops nonchalantly onto the speaker cabinet, and starts sticking pencils! Yes pencils, into his ears, nose, and mouth.

He takes the pencils one by one and begins to scribble on the guitar strings, as if he’s taking notes. But he is not just screwing around, he really plays! Bounding pencils off the strings, hitting strings for a high staccato sound, playing backwards, upside down. He is manic! What fun he is to see!
This is definitely the most accomplished, the most fun, the most exciting band in New York!

div.p: Went to CBGB’s to catch this band. The club is full although the weather stinks. We wade through the crowd to find seats near the wall. You can’t get near the stage here. You gotta sit down. Is this real?

Come On is a young, five-piece band. All are wearing white dress shirts, black pants and white sneakers. Succinct…They look like high school students for the most part, and probably are. Smart & clean.
Their music is a bit reggae, a bit rock, a bit conceptual; experimenting with changes in rhythm and timing.
The lead singer is a good-looking collegiate type kid with horn-rimmed glasses. He sings in a stilted, staccato voice as if he’s having a fit. Pumping his knees; a spastic march in time.

Their guitarist is forgettable. A good rhythm guitar. She reflects the deadpan look of the band. Strong drummer. Their music is Devo-ish, Talking Heads-influenced. Yet originality and humor shine through.

The singer is having artistic spasms.. His face turns red; he sings all the words he can with one breath. You sweat it out with him. His hands in fists, moving like a machine near his body. He pedals like a machine near his body. He pedals with his legs bent at the knees.
The lyrics form a hologram of American blandness. The lyrics are hilarious. Slice-of-life. The singer beats his chest. His hands contorted into fists. An autistic child?
Probably their funniest song is a slap at one of America’s institutions: Disneyland. Like a child wailing at the disappointment of reality:
He delivers it as a tirade; an out-of-breath conversation. Like a victim of reality shock therapy. The best male vocalist I have seen in a while.
At the end he is like an exhausted child. All the tantrums gone. All the visions spent. A band to evoke images of Ladies Home Journal.
It’ll sell in the midwest……

div.p: A late word from Virgin Records is that Barry Andrews has left XTC to persue a solo career. The band remains together, and the split was said to be amicable.

This interview was done in the dining room of the Gramercy Park Hotel. The resturant was not happy that we were there, and proceeded to make it difficult for us. Barry and I had to repeatedly tell the waiters what we wanted. It made for a bit of an uncomfortable atmosphere. But we survived.
Barry has an extremely dry sense of humor, which was well served admist the frowning waiters.
S:How long have you been playing together?
B:This line-up about two years
S:Where are you from?
B:We're all from Swindon. I was born in London, but moved to Swindon. The others are born and bred
S:Is that near London?

B:It's 80 miles down the motorway. It's an appalling little town known only for railways. I thought you'd know that. It's like a jke in the music papers that we come from Swindon. It's a notoriously un-hip place to come from.
S:Doesn't everyone come from un-hip places and migrate to hip places?
B:Sometimes. That's why we didnt use to cut it with the London music industry, 'cause we were up from the country.
S:Did Did you choose whhat hotel you were going to stay at, or did they just put you here?
B:This is quite good actually, though you wouldn't guess it.
S:This is for the professional hotel person, I think.
B:That's what we are.
S:Do you get tired of being on the road?

B:Yeah, I do. Exept when there's novelty to sustain it, like there is in America, 'cause we've never been here before. Same old clubs, do the same old things night after night can be tiring. It's virtually exhausting.
S:What would you rather do? Would you rather just record and then play certain dates, as opposed to....

B: No, no. I do like gigging when it's done in the right way, I think. But when you just do loads and loads of dates all bound together, on top of each other--which is the only way really you can make it pay, make it pay for itself.....
S:So you wake up and you don't exactly know where you are...
B:You wake up in the night and think youre in a different city..
S:So you do one night stands?
B:Yeah, they're all one night.
S:Youve been doing that for two years?
B:On and off..making albums.
S:DO you like doing that?
B:I like bits of that. All things considered it's not a bad job at all...Beats the shit out of factories.
S:More creativity.
B:To a degree.
S:It seems Brittish bands have less trouble being signed than American bands.
B:There was a big spate of internet around about the time we got signed..They were signing anything that mved the year before last.
S:Did you want to sign?
B:Oh yeah. Anyway we could make money out of it. Enough to live on anyway.
S:Has Virgin treated you well? Given you what you wanted?

B:Always. They're as good as they can be. The only times we have arguments, is when we can't agree between the 4 of us what to do. Then the record company more or less takes over and does the most commerically viable thing they can do under the circumstances.
S:The company is supporting you on this tour?
B:They're paying for it.
S:That's nice of them.
B:Foolhearty of 'em.
S:Have your records done well?
B:No, they've bombed out.
S:How do you feel about that?
B:A bit desperate.
S:Is it bad publicity? Is it that the music isn't accessible for
S:So you think it's only music like the Ramones, which is so blatent, so clear, That people have something to grab on to?
B:Pop music is about that.
S:You define yourself as a pop band

B:Yeah. I don't see us as anything more. I think it's quite a noble call. Being a pop band. (Here I am introduced to Colin Moulding, bass player....Barry comments on the waiters:"This place is really fascist...")
S:But if all music was Blondie and the Ramones it would be boring. Your music balances that.

B:I don't think it should all be like that. On the other hand, to do that unsuccessfully is a failure, isn't it. And to try and not do that and yet still not come up aith anything atristically valid is a failure as well.

div.head: CLEM BURKE
TALKS TO Neil Hubbard
div.p: This interview (of sorts) was done after Blondie’s last appearance here. The inevitable party took place in Jeri and Paul’s swank Ave. apartment.. Throughout the interview guitars are being bashed in the background, noses are being blown, and a lotta beer gets guzzled. So, 2, 3, 4......
CLEM: It’s good seein’ you guys again–like you, and Jerri....
NEIL: Truthfully, I was kinda surprised you remembered.. Like me and ya know, all the other people...
CLEM: Naahhh. I remember you guys.
NEIL: Well, I thought since then you've been all these different places....

CLEM: But we were never back here since then. No I remembered you guys were really nice to us. That was only about a year and half ago, but we should have played here at least two or three times since then.
NEIL: What did you do instead? Go to Europe?

CLEM: Well, after the Iggy tour we spend almost all our time in Europe. We did three weeks with the Kinks in the south. That was great.. Everyday going to see Ray Davies. Everyday you got to see the Kinks and talk to ‘em.
NEIL: It’s better than touring with Iggy, huh?

CLEM: I don’t know. Less attitude, I guess… A different sort of attitude. All the English rock stars like that kind of have this attitude like they accept us. Truthfully, in England, we’re like T.Rex or the first stage of the Beatles, or the Kinks, or Herman's Hermits. Who?? Everybody in England reads the music papers and see what’s on Top of the Pops. They regard us as like this young band that has hit records that’s going through all this shit that they went through. When we met them it was almost like a big brother trip.
NEIL: They were nice to you?

CLEM: They’re real nice, ‘cause on their level, on and English level, we’ve made it. In ‘64 and ‘65 there was a year or eighteen months where every single of those guys (Kinks) put out went in the Top 10. We had four Top 5 singles–Number One–in England.
NEIL: Which was number one?
CLEM: “Denis”. That was the biggest seller—600,000
NEIL: Aren’t the royalty rates higher there?

CLEM: No. Our royalty rate is half because we’re signed to an American company. The hippest thing is what Devo did. Deco signed to two record companies. They’re signed to Warners in American and to Virgin in Europe. So when they go to Europe, they only have to deal with Virgin, and when they’re in America they only have to deal with Warners. It’s two separate entities, and it involves making one album and getting advances.

Being signed directly means being signed like an English band—-where your royalty rate isn’t chopped. If you sign to an American company that has a liscence or subsidiary company overseas, the royalty rate is cut in half That sort of fucks you up financially.

But Devo pulled off the best deal of all times. Business-wise they pulled it off! They told Warners they’d sign here for world-wide distribution. They gave Warners their word on that. Meanwhile they go to England to do a tour, Virgin approaches them, and they sign to Virgin. Then they came back to America and told Warners: “Look, we’re already signed in Europe.” It’s really exceptional what they pulled off.
NEIL: Why do so many records come out in England that you have to get as imports here?

CLEM: That’s in the record companies in America. People like Paul Weller are really pessimistic about ever having any great deal of success in America. They feel that they’re just an English entity. They get alot of that kind of shit from the record companies over here. They signed world-wide, but they signed by the way of England. The label here has the option of putting their record out or not....If they don’t feel like putting it out, they don’t have to put it out. (As in the case of C.B.S. and the CLASH–ED.)
NEIL: And even if they do release it here it’s with minimal push of promo.

CLEM: I’m doing this thing that’s very premature and it could happen in a year or so, it’s hard to say. ‘Cause it’s like if our next album dosen’t do really good in America, the record company might drop us.
NEIL: But isn’t it largely their fault in the long run?
CLEM: No. Record companies can only do so much.....
NEIL: So can a band.....

CLEM: This idea will flip you out. It’s sort of confidential, but it dosen’t matter. I always have like this weird goal…Like: wouldn’t that be nice? I have been trying to put this band together, in a year or two years… like with Paul Weller from the Jam. Me and him are friends. And Eric Faulkner and Glen Matlock and me. As an ex-journalist, what would you say if you heard there was a band with me, Faulkner, Matlock, and Weller?
NEIL: It’d be incredible! Like some superstar reunion!

CLEM: It would escalate things. Not so say anybody’s…. Eric Faulkner is legitimate. But everyone else is sort of foundering, or cult or whatever. I saw Glen when he was playing with Sid Vicious. It was them and Rat Scabies and Steve Newell from the Rich Kids.. Glen writes good songs, and he’s a really, really good bass player.
NEIL: He’s a lot better than Sid was.
CLEM: Sid Vicious isn’t a bass player. But you should have seen this gig. Kinda like the thing I’m talking about. Hype-wise it would be incredible.

In 1963 I was thirteen. My mom was a country-western singer and I was a farmboy. Also, the Beatles happened… KJR was Radio Free Europe for the refugees out in Duvall. To be honest, it took another year or so for this particular farmkid to catch on to the fact that there was a historic change happening.

When I was in third grade in Sedro Wolley, living next to the movie House where “Love Me Tender” and “King Creole” played, Elvis was my main muse. Dancing in front of mom's stereo to "Hound Dog" and "Don't Be Cruel".. groovin’ to the Big Bopper, Bobby Darin, Fats Domino and Buddy Holly (the skinny kid with the glasses) on the radio, I had sanction.
Mom took me to hear her sing one Night because I learned the Presley Two-Step (one forward and one back).

But the Beatles, she told me, were awful. Dad watched the Stones on Ed Sullivan with us, and said, “I can see why they’re called dirty. It’s not dirt, it’s Filth!” No sanction. But all the time on my Packard-Bell portable, up in my little room, I was groovin’! To the Folkies. I was enraptured and romanced by Simon’s “I Am A Rock”, and “Young Girls Are Coming To The Canyon” with the Mamas & Papas Dylan, yea. And somehow, when Dylan picked up an electric guitar I wasn’t aware of any outrage. I was down in the barnyard, making those sounds with my mouth.
And I knew those Beatles couldn’t be as awful as mom said. “I Wanna Hold Your Hand” was the Truth to this throbbing pubescent mind.

Unbeknownst to me, the youth, and quite a few of the grown-ups in Seattle, Bellevue, Kirkland were on fire —Rock N Roll was the wave of the future again. And I met them on the traditional meeting ground for city and country: The county fair.

I was in 4-H, of course, and I had a pet Jersey cow to lead around. Every year we’d go to at least the Monroe county fair and the King County Fair in Enumclaw. Although Enumclaw was the biggest fair, I believe all The hip action was in Monroe.

There was, of course, the rodeo…. horse shows, cow shows, and pie shows Vacuum cleaners, window cleaners, floor cleaners, and organ grinders. But there was also stock car races. And when there weren’t cars on the track the fail officials had found it lucrative to bring half-a-dozen Seattle rock bands to play for free—----there at the racetrack.

Little did they know the ultimate terror they would help bring upon Washington parents everywhere, as their kids became Rock N Rollers, and forgot about doing the dishes and/or feeding the calves. (I noticed they had this much rock n roll only that one year. After that they got all the old country stars they could find).

I must have shoved cow watch onto every kid in the club, so me (I was the president) and Rick DeVries (he’s the vice-president), could go and goggle at Lucky and the Gamblers, the Liverpool Five, and numerous other tatty costumed bands. Everybody looked like Paul Revere and the Raiders… everybody in pseudo-Carnaby Street duds. And Merilee Rush> and the Turnabouts––two shows daily on the midway. I was in love with her overbite.

And there was this scheme which now seems out of a dream. In a tent in some accidental corner of the fairgrounds, kids from Greater Seattle burbs—I swear—were having honest-to-god sanctioned, amateur Battle of the bands. Thirteen year old, sixteen year old Johnny Rays and leather Elvis’s—- tight blue jeans and greasy curls, were climbing onto this little plywood stage with their Fenders and Gibsons and singing “House of the Rising Sun” while their mothers were crawling around in their nylons and Jackie Kennedy coats arranging and checking power cords. What!!??

figure.figDesc: Collage of text and images, newspaper headlines and images of musicians.

div.p: No kidding. It was like a 4-H club for Rock N Roll. Really, I was out there. I don’t know if they won the chance to be backup band for the Bands at PLU, or if they got to cut a single, or if they just got a new set of strings. But the point is, they were playing rock n roll, and their mothers were not only watching, but brushing their greasy hair before they went on stage. Sanction!

They weren’t as “good”, of course, as the “Professionals” out on the race track; nor did they get the money or attention that Merilee Rush (who would pick up her watch to see how much longer the set was—right in the middle of “Angel Of The Morning”) got… but they felt real-er. They were me, living my dream. They seemed to be not only supported, but even pushed by their mothers to perform and live out that dream.
Sanction.

div.p: POLY: In the new wave I only like the Pistols, apart from us. And Reggae. I was brought up on Reggae 'cause I came from Brixton.
NEVA: Why do you think Reggae has become so popular with punks?

POLY: Well, I like Reggae anyway ‘cause I'm half black, and I grew up in a black area and was brought up on it... So I can’t judge it by what other punks say in any case. But punk and Reggae are the same in the sense that they're basic...Reggae is a very basic music, it's not very technical, the rhythm rules it. It's got its own little language, its own little scene... But it's changed a lot from Ska and Blue Beat, now it's got heavily into Dub and Rastafarian influences. It’s more cultural. There's a lot of fakes in it too, ‘cause if you're a real Rasta you're not meant to show your locks, you keep them under a hat unless you're praying.
NEVA: How old were you when you left home?

POLY: Fifteen. I just moved around for a year, mostly living in squats. I stayed with junkies for a little while. I didn't really like it very much but I didn't have nowhere else to live. There's no flats available for young single people, it's one of the worst problems in London. It's virtually impossible to get somewhere to live, it really is, unless you've got a load of money. These council flats won't let single people in.

div.head: EYES OPEN?
div.p: There are many things wrong with the record industry. Any conscious record consumer knows this. But 99% of the record buyers in the world are unconscious.

What this piece amounts to is a bitch session, my personal gripes; laid out in a somewhat random fashion--maybe somewhat carelessly--but the point is clear: There are far too many things being done wrong for one person to change, it is now a matter of raising everyone's level of awareness about the fucked up state of the recording business.

With albums hitting the market at an inflated list price of $8.98 per disc, new groups--the contemporary progressive groups (not progressive in the sense of "techno rock") have a limited chance of making a hit. As record consumers become more and more anesthetized by such high selling, high priced releases as the $12 .98 list Saturday Night Fever, they willingly assimilate the higher priced single LP's. I deny S.N.F.'s existence on its price alone!!!

The high number of sales of a record that retails for at least $8.98 (usually more) shows that people have been irrevocably conditioned to pay astronomical prices for inferior pressings of inferior music. One thing to say for disco listeners is that they openly recognize the inferiority of their music. They openly admit it. "All we wanna do is dance dance, dance."

Most disco records are hot sellers for about two or three weeks, then they are stiffed into oblivion. Some disco records however, employ advanced production techniques. This is good, but actually a technique nicked from the German “psychedelic” musicians of the early and middle seventies: Neu, Cluster, and Kraftwerk.

The disco format has allowed this new music to be presented in a marketable pop format, Some of the recent disco records are almost tantalizing from a production standpoint alone--Donna Summer’s "I Feel Love", for instance. I'd rather have a Nick Lowe or Brian Eno production on any record.

To get back to the point. Consumers are idiots. Do they buy records for the sake of its art, or do they buy it because everyone else does? It is rather difficult to have totally original taste in music. People are hesitant to buy a record they haven't heard before, unless it's by their favorite artist (whether or not that fave lost it five years ago is of no concern). I don't know that many people buy a record based upon reading a review.

The Clash and Lol Creme/Kevin Godley’s "L" have received much critical acclaim, but have sold few albums in this area. Reviews are sometimes "bought" by a record label--either to stimulate sales, or merely to service the press. By exchanging "favors of gratitude" with a writer to do a good review, they buy a sense of security. They're more concerned with radio play. After all, it is where the mass market is.

To change the buying habits of those aillions who bought Fleetwood Mac or Peter Frampton or Saturday Night Fever is like trying to activate a dormant volcano by mortal means. They are comfortable as conformist sheep. To wake them up would shatter their American Dream: Ignorance.

Until then, you can do something. Refuse to buy $8.98 list single albums. Imports are an exception. Their pressing quality is generally superior, and most of the profound music of today is available only in import form.

Artists like Billy Joel, Barbara Streisand, Boston, Steve Miller, Ted Nugent, and Chicago are knowingly allowing their labels to shove their corporate prick up all our asses, Fuck them! Fuck Barbara Streisand and all her "little people” They ought to have the human instinct, alledging themselves to be "artists", to refuse to record and release a record at such prices. They're as openly barbaric as their company presidents and A&R Jerks. It's their profit, as well as

the record company's. Obviously, these types of people are not artists, but profiteers. Modern day carpetbaggers. Hooligan racketeers who tour the world collecting money by the ream. Literally, they're cornholing brown-nosed dick lickers!

This is the situation today. There are plenty of influential musicians who are lucky enough to have Top 100 albums. Of all the new wave artists to release LP's since 1976 (and there are alot of them), only a few have reached a top chart position in the U.S. Patti Smith, Blondie, and the Ramones have all broken through on a limited basis. But consider this: Elvis Costello is the only British new vave artist to be lucky enough to have sold an appreciable number of LP's in the states. Few have actually toured besides Costello, except for scattered dates in the media cities—N.Y., L.A., S.F Cleveland, Detroit, etc.

To wit: Many bands (Clash, Stranglers, Boomtown Rats, Jam, Ultravox, Costello, Generation X, ad infinitum) have been touring Great Britian and Europe for up to three years. Slogging back and forth to small gigs in little towns. But they have support. Possibly because Europe, and England specifically, are more conducive to a greater outgrowth of not only creative impulses, but corporate benevolence.

Throughout history (Gawd! This is sounding heavy!), artists have survived no matter how barely, by receiving grants & benefits from the church, guild, royalty and other wealthy individuals. This feeling is maintained even today. By observing record company signings and promotion activity in Europe, it is easy to see how little risk U.S. record companies are willing to take on a new act, Not another re-working of someone else's broken dreams. Bands like Pink Floyd, Led Zepplin, Fleetwood Mac, Deep Purple, Black Sabbath, ad nauseam, are rarely---if ever---covered by British trade papers. They have completely lost their credibility. They may as well not exist.

Europeans recognize the need to indulge art. It is in their blood. The shit groups mentioned above are still rather large sellers in the U.S., but not in their home countries. They are dead meat. The English rock scene has replenished itself constantly for the last 10-15 years. Good things have been, will and are coming of it. There's been a lot of shit moozik, but a definite mark has been sighted. Industry must bust soon and allow young talent--all the good ones, to make it.
It boils down to that. A total destruction and subsequent restructuring of the whole record industry. And, it is your job (since you bothered to read
this) to do everything in your power to destroy and change it.
To the front!
